dok_rationale: Part (c) coordinates sample structure, inferential target, hypotheses, shared expected counts, and conditions to adjudicate a procedure claim and explain why identical arithmetic does not imply identical population meaning.
stem: Suppose a transit authority obtains the shown counts under either design.\par\smallskip \textbf{Design A:} Take independent SRSs of 100 from each of three route populations of 4,000 and record ticket method.\par \textbf{Design B:} Take one SRS of 300 from 15,000 system riders and record both route and ticket method.\par\smallskip \textbf{Ari:} ``Route rows imply homogeneity; the counts are enough to choose.''\par \textbf{Bea:} ``Read how riders were sampled; identical counts can support different population claims.''
first_take: Which claim is more defensible? Cite the sampling structure of each design.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: For each design, state the number of random samples and the categorical variable or variables recorded.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the expected counts and $df$, then verify random sampling, 10 percent, and expected counts for both designs.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Adjudicate the claims. For each design, name the procedure and state $H_0$ and $H_a$ in context. Use the sampling structure, diagnose the rejected table-only rule, and identify the numerical pieces that remain identical.

answers.a: Design A uses three independent SRSs and records one categorical response, ticket method. Design B uses one SRS and records two categorical variables, route and ticket method.
answers.b: Each row has expected counts $(50,30,20)$, all greater than 5, and $df=(3-1)(3-1)=4$. For A, the independent SRSs satisfy $100\leq0.10(4{,}000)=400$ in each route population. For B, the SRS satisfies $300\leq0.10(15{,}000)=1{,}500$.
answers.c: Bea is warranted. For A, use homogeneity: $H_0$ says ticket-method distributions are the same across route populations; $H_a$ says at least one differs. For B, use independence: $H_0$ says route and ticket method are not associated among system riders; $H_a$ says they are associated. Three route-population SRSs versus one system SRS with two variables controls the choice. The rejected rule falsely assumes separate population samples for B. Observed and expected counts, $df=4$, the statistic, and p-value match; their population meanings differ.

expectedElements.description: Names homogeneity for A and independence for B
States same-distribution and no-association hypotheses in context
Uses three population SRSs versus one two-variable SRS
Diagnoses the table-only rule's false sampling assumption

scoringGuide.E: Names both tests and hypotheses, uses sampling structure, diagnoses the rejected rule, and identifies shared arithmetic.
scoringGuide.P: Distinguishes the tests but omits hypothesis context, the consequence, or shared arithmetic.
scoringGuide.I: Chooses from row labels alone or says the designs need different expected counts.
